# Reading the auth audit log

`GET /v1/audit` answers who did what and when on the deployment. It records key
creates, revokes and rotates, every access attempt with its mode, and every
denial with its reason. Reading it is itself a gated action.

```bash
export BASE=http://127.0.0.1:8080
audit() { curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" "$BASE/v1/audit$1"; }
```

## Provoke some records

```bash
rimsky auth init --endpoint "$BASE"
rimsky auth create-key --endpoint "$BASE" --key "$ADMIN" --name reader  --role read-only
rimsky auth create-key --endpoint "$BASE" --key "$ADMIN" --name doomed  --role read-only
rimsky auth create-key --endpoint "$BASE" --key "$ADMIN" --name rotated --role read-only
rimsky auth revoke doomed  --endpoint "$BASE" --key "$ADMIN"
rimsky auth rotate rotated --endpoint "$BASE" --key "$ADMIN" --grace 24h

# an executed write, then the same write as a dry run
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -X POST "$BASE/v1/templates" -d "$SPEC"
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN" -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  -X POST "$BASE/v1/templates?dry_run=true" -d "$SPEC"

# three kinds of refusal
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer $READER" -X POST "$BASE/v1/templates" -d "$SPEC"   # 403
curl -sS "$BASE/v1/instances"                                                          # 401
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer rk_notarealkey..." "$BASE/v1/instances"              # 401
```

## Read them back

```bash
audit "?limit=500"
```

Five record kinds appear: `auth.key_created`, `auth.key_revoked`,
`auth.key_rotated`, `auth.access_attempted`, `auth.access_denied`.

Each record carries what an operator needs to attribute it.

- `auth.key_created`, `auth.key_revoked` and `auth.key_rotated` name the key by
  `payload.key_name`.
- `auth.access_attempted` carries `payload.mode` and `payload.executed`. The
  dry-run write is recorded as `dry_run` with `executed: false`; the real write
  as `execute` with `executed: true`.
- `auth.access_denied` carries `payload.denial_reason`, which distinguishes
  `invalid_token`, `no_token` and `permission_denied`. A refusal for a bad
  credential is not confused with a refusal for a credential that was not
  allowed to do that.

## Narrow it

The route accepts nine filters, and each narrows.

```bash
audit "?kind=auth.key_created"
audit "?key_name=reader&limit=500"
audit "?action=template:register&limit=500"
audit "?action_prefix=auth:&limit=500"
audit "?target=/v1/templates&limit=500"
audit "?status=403&limit=500"
audit "?mode=dry_run&limit=500"
audit "?since=2026-08-16T00:00:00Z"
audit "?limit=1"
```

`?limit` returns a `next_cursor`; pass it back as `?limit=1&cursor=$CUR` to page
forward.

A mistyped filter is refused rather than quietly matching nothing. A `kind`
outside the auth set — say `state_transition` — answers 400, and a `since` that
is not RFC3339 — say `yesterday` — answers 400. An operator learns about the
typo instead of reading a misleadingly empty log.

## Reading the audit is gated

```bash
curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H "Authorization: Bearer $READER"  "$BASE/v1/audit"
# 200 — the read-only role carries audit:read

curl -sS -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -H "Authorization: Bearer $NOAUDIT" "$BASE/v1/audit"
# 403 — a key without audit:read
```

The log that records who did what is not a way around the permissions it
records.
